performers: Isaac Stern, violin; Symphony of the Air; Leonard Bernstein
recorded: 19 April 1956, New York; Columbia ML 5144 issued 1956
intro: Isaac Stern, who was the soloist at the first performance in 1954, plays the first movement of Bernstein’s violin Serenade (after Plato’s Symposium), with Bernstein conducting. The movement opens with a slow fugato for the soloist, followed by a fast sonata-allegro on the same material.

sections.label: A · Lento, solo violin begins fugato
B · Allegro marcato, Pausanias
sections.mNote: Sonata-allegro built on the opening fugato.

cues.title: Opening fugato, solo violin
cues.text: The Serenade opens with a fugato begun by the solo violin. Bernstein’s guide links it to Phaedrus’s “lyrical oration in praise of Eros”. The intervals and contours of the violin’s opening return in the later movements.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s guideposts of 8 August 1954 for each movement, and the account of the opening theme, on the Leonard Bernstein Office page for the Serenade. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/23/serenade-after-platos-symposium
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bernstein on Plato’s Symposium
cues.text: Bernstein said the Serenade resulted from “a rereading of Plato’s charming dialogue”, The Symposium, and had “no literal program”. He described the music as “a series of related statements in praise of love”.
cues.evidence: Quotations from Bernstein on the Leonard Bernstein Office page for the Serenade. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/23/serenade-after-platos-symposium

cues.title: Pausanias, Allegro marcato
cues.text: The Allegro marcato follows the speech of Pausanias on the duality of lover and beloved. It is a classical sonata-allegro on the material of the opening fugato. In the second theme the violin plays disjunct grace-note figures and dissonant intervals.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s guideposts of 8 August 1954, on the Bernstein Office page; the sentence on the second theme is the Office’s bracketed gloss to the guideposts. The change of tempo at about 3:03 is placed from the audio, which changes character at that point. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/23/serenade-after-platos-symposium
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording, New York, 1956
cues.text: Isaac Stern, soloist at the first performance in Venice on 12 September 1954, recorded the Serenade with Bernstein in New York on 19 April 1956. Columbia issued it that year as a mono LP.
cues.evidence: Premiere: Bernstein Office page. Recording date, mono recording and 1956 release: Sony’s upload of the Eryximachus movement. Carrier, ML 5144: Discogs, and a Columbia advertisement in The American Record Guide, November 1956. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/23/serenade-after-platos-symposium https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vZ6lhjkhZk0 https://www.discogs.com/release/5995545 https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1956-11_23_3

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial publication in 1956, before 1963; Columbia advertised ML 5144 as newly issued in The American Record Guide of November 1956
fields.note: The American Record Guide for November 1956 carries a Columbia advertisement listing the Serenade, ML 5144, at $3.98 among five Bernstein recordings “issued for the first time”, and the December 1956 issue lists it again. Discogs and the Internet Archive date the LP to 1956, and Sony’s reissue note says ‘Originally released 1956’. The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not US or worldwide clearance, not a Creative Commons licence and not a US-government recording. Rights in the composition are separate.

composer.background:
Leonard Bernstein was born on 25 August 1918 in Lawrence, Massachusetts, the eldest of three children of Samuel and Jennie Bernstein, Jewish immigrants from Ukraine. The family moved to Boston when he was a few months old, and his father sold hairdressing and beauty supplies. In the autumn of 1928 an aunt gave the family an upright piano, and the ten-year-old Leonard began to pick out songs on it. Samuel Bernstein, who wanted his son to join the business, agreed to lessons. The New Yorker reported in 1958 that he had said backstage at Tanglewood: “someday I suppose the books will say, ‘Lenny Bernstein had a father.’” In October 1932 Bernstein began lessons with Helen Coates, an assistant to the Boston pianist Heinrich Gebhard.

He attended Boston Latin School and entered Harvard in 1935, where his teachers included Walter Piston and Edward Burlingame Hill. In January 1937 he met the conductor Dimitri Mitropoulos at a reception and spent the following week at Mitropoulos’s Boston Symphony rehearsals. On 14 November of that year he met Aaron Copland at a dance recital in New York. He graduated in June 1939.
